RESPONDENT

NATHANSON, J.
:

The parties have entered into a separation agreement
in which they have agreed to all aspects of their pending divorce except:
division of assets, maintenance, and one facet of the religious upbringing of
the children (namely, whether they are required to have bar mitzvahs). Those
three issues will now be decided.

The parties were married in 1983. The husband is 41
and the wife is 35 years old. There are 2 children of the marriage: Joshua
Michael, born April 16, 1984, and Geoffrey Stephen, born July 1, 1987. The
older boy has started school; the younger boy is at home with his mother and
attends a day care center where she works.

The wife was married previously. There were no
children of that brief union. She was employed and self‑supporting at the
time and, therefore, did not seek maintenance.

The husband is a veterinarian practising in
Dartmouth. He is a partner in Harbour Cities Veterinary Associates, entitled to
a 1/4 share of the partnership.

She trained and graduated as a registered nurse in
Ontario. Subsequently, she worked as a nurse in Nova Scotia. Between September,
1980, and December, 1982, she worked as a nursing assistant at the Northwood
Senior Citizens' Centre. She injured her back while assisting a patient there.
Her registration in Nova Scotia has lapsed. For that reason and because of her
injured back, she says that she is unable to qualify and work again as a nurse.
She works part‑time in children's day care centers, and says that she is
willing to work full time but has been unable to find a full‑time job.

The parties separated on April 28, 1989.

DIVISION OF ASSETS

The statements of property filed by the parties
disclose the following assets owned as of the date of separation: matrimonial
home, 2 vehicles, household furnishings and effects, registered retirement
savings plans (R.R.S.P.s), securities, insurance, and the husband's partnership
interest. As well, the wife claims that an amount which she received in 1988 as
the result of a decision of the Workers' Compensation Appeal Board is an
exempted asset.

Each of these assets must be valued and categorized
individually.

Matrimonial Home
. This property is situated at 18 Farquharson
Street, Dartmouth. The parties have agreed upon a valuation of $110,000. It is
subject to a mortgage, the present balance of which is agreed to be $68,000.

Vehicles
. The parties have agreed that the 1986 Hyundai Pony which she owns and
drives has a present net value of $1,500, and that the 1988 Dodge Caravan which
he owns and drives has a present gross value of $12,500 and is subject to a
dealer plan loan having a present balance of $17,671.

Household Furnishings and Effects
. The parties have divided these items between them
and have agreed that the items in her possession have a value of $6,000 and the
items in his possession have a value of $1,000.

R.R.S.P.s
. The only remaining plan appears to have a value of approximately
$725; the parties have not seen fit to provide any additional information. If
cashed, this amount would attract income tax of not less than 30%. Another
plan, in the amount of some $19,000, was cashed in by the husband after
separation and the proceeds used to pay $11,250 to his parents and the balance
to income tax. There is disagreement as to whether his parents made a gift or a
loan of $10,000 in order to help them purchase the matrimonial home; he alleges
that it was a loan and that this payment constituted re‑payment of that
loan plus some interest; she alleges that it was a gift and that this payment
is part of a process of denuding himself of assets. A letter from him to his
parents, exhibited at trial, dated about the time of the purchase of the
matrimonial home, indicates that the money from his parents was intended as a loan
re‑payable with interest. I so find.

Securities
. He testified that he sold 1,000 shares of something called Stratas
for a total price of $63, and he holds 10 options of Nova which have now
expired. She testified that she holds 4 $100 Canada Savings Bonds in the names
of the children, and he testifed that he also has 'some of them'. I find that
all such bonds are held in trust for the chldren. Other securities and 100
ounces of silver appear to have been disposed of.

Insurance
. His statement of property discloses. that he has 3 policies of life
and disability insurance, in the face amounts of $100,000 each, with the wife
named as beneficiary. Since these are term coverages, they do not have any cash
surrender value.

Partnership Interest
. He estimates the value of his 1/4 interest at
$62,500, an amount which is somewhat higher than the $50,000 which was paid to
buy out another partner in the recent past. She claims a ½ share of his 1/4 interest on the grounds that she
helped out in the clinic, decorated the upstairs apartment where they lived for
a time, stayed home and cared for the children while he worked, and co‑signed
loans all of which have now been re‑financed. He testified about
outstanding business loans presently totalling some $47,000; it is not clear
from the evidence whether his estimate of the value of his share is or is not
net of this indebtedness. I find that this asset, unlike the other assets
enumerated, is a business asset, and is not a matrimonial asset.

Workers' Compensation Payment
. The wife submits that the $15,000 award is
excluded from the definition of matrimonial assets set out in s.4(1)(b) of the
Matrimonial
Property Act
, 1980 which provides that "an award or settlement of
damages in court in favour of one spouse" is excepted from matrimonial
assets. This submission assumes that such an award of worker's compensation by
the Board is the equivalent of an award or settlement of damages by a court. On
the other hand, it is submitted on behalf of the husband that workers'
compensation is a statutory scheme to compensate workers for lost income
resulting from injuries sustained in the workplace; that the award by the Board
was therefore intended to compensate her for lost income rather than future
loss; that the lump sum awarded to her was in replacement of an accumulation of
payments which would have been paid during the course of the marriage to
compensate the wife for her inability or reduced ability to earn income; that
the funds which have built up in her bank account are the same as an
accumulaton of funds saved from earnings; and that there is no reason why the
wife should be excused from having to contribute her earnings, or her
compensation for lost earnings, to the matrimonial pot, any more than the husband
could have set aside part of his earnings in a savings account and claimed that
they were not matrimonial assets.

The submission of the wife is not accepted. I find
that an award of compensation is not the equivalent of an award or settlement
of damages in court. If it were, s.4(2) of the
Act
would apply:

"'
matrimonial
assets' defined

4  ...

Damages
or insurance proceeds

(2) Notwithstanding clauses (b) and
(c) of sub‑section (1), an award or settlement of damages in court or
money being paid or payable under an insurance policy is a matrimonial asset to
the extent that it is made, paid or payable in respect of a matrimonial
asset."

In
such case, I would further find that such an award is wholly a matrimonial
asset because it was made and paid in respect of income which, if accumulated
in an account, would be a matrimonial asset. I accept the submission made on
behalf of the husband.

In accordance with the foregoing discussion, I find
that the matrimonial assets of the parties are as enumerated and allocated as
follows:

This is a convenient place to note the debts of the parties
over and above the mortgage against the matrimonial home, the charge against
the husband's vehicle, and the loan from his parents (which has now been
repaid). The statement of property filed in 1989 by the husband discloses
personal debts of $1,500 and business debts totalling $47,431. The statement of
property filed in 1989 by the wife discloses no debts.

The wife claims an unequal division of matrimonial
assets. She submits that the husband has business assets and the ability to
earn higher income in the years ahead. While the value of the business assets
appears to be offset to a substantial extent by the amount of the husband's
business debts, the Court takes note that the wife will have the care and
custody of the children of the marriage who will have needs which must be
provided for Section 13 of the
Matrimonial Property Act
authorizes the
Court to make an unequal division of matrimonial assets or a division of
property that is not matrimonial assets. In the present circumstances, it would
be very difficult, if not impossible, to divide the partnership interest which
is the only non‑matrimonial asset. An equal division of matrimonial
assets would be unfair in light of the facts stated and the factors set out in
s.13(b) and (h) of the
Act
.

The wife seeks an 80%/20% split of assets. The Court
has come to the conclusion that a 70%/30% split would be appropriate in the
circumstances of this particular case.

The wife will retain the balance of the compensation
award, her vehicle and her share of household effects. The husband will retain
the R.R.S.P., his vehicle (being responsible for payment of the indebtedness
associated with it), and his share of household effects. The matrimonial home
will be sold at a price as close as possible to market value and, after payment
of the mortgage balance and all costs of sale, the net proceeds will be divided
between the parties in such manner as will give full effect to the foregoing
split of matrimonial assets.

MAINTENANCE

The statement of financial information filed by the
husband discloses that he earns $5,750 per month and that he spends $6,641 per
month, for a monthly deficit of $891. The statement also discloses that the
husband expects a reduction of his gross earnings in 1990‑91 of
approximately $500 per month while, at the same time, his expenditures will
increase to $7,451, for a projected monthly deficit of $2,201. A review of the
items making up the list of proposed expenditures reveals a number of items
which are related to payment of the business debts, which must be paid if his
ability to earn income is to be maintained, as well as other items which are
either excessive or discretionary and must be stringently reduced.

The statement of financial information filed by the
wife discloses that she earns $305.05 per month, receives family allowance of
$65.48 and maintenance of $1,800, for a total income of $2,170.53. The
statement also discloses present expenditures of $3,550 per month. Thus, the
wife has a monthly deficit of $1,380. Proposed budget figures are not included
in the statement. A review of the list of actual current expenditures reveals a
number of items which may have been normal and reasonable while the parties
were living together with their children as a single family unit, but which now
must be reduced or eliminated altogether.

It used to be stated, as one factor tending to
favour contemplated marriages, that 2 people could live together more cheaply
than one. I have no doubt that, generally speaking, such a statement was true.
It remains true today. Its corollary is that 2 people cannot live separately as
cheaply as they can live together. That corollary is applicable here. Both
parties must reduce their expenditures. They can do that only by lowering their
standards of living. In the present case, that must be done to a substantial
degree. It is impossible for monthly gross incomes totalling $5,615 to support
expenditures of some $11,000.

The wife claims spousal and child support. The
husband has been voluntarily paying $1,800 per month on a without prejudice
basis, but says that he has been going further into debt in order to do so. The
wife submits that she and the children are entitled to a higher level of
support.

Both sides rely upon the provisions of the
Divorce
Act
, 1985
dealing with corollary relief and, in particular, the provisions
of
s.15(5)
,
(7)
and
(8)
.

Sub‑section (5) directs the Court to consider
"the condition, means, needs and other circumstances" of each spouse
and child. One of the objectives of an order for support of a spouse enumerated
in s‑s.(7) is stated to be: "(d) in so far as practicable, promote
the economic self‑sufficiency of each spouse within a reasonable period
of time." The objectives of an order for support of a child are stated in
s‑s.(8) to be:

"COROLLARY RELIEF

15        ...

(8)          ...

(a)

recognize that the spouses have a
joint financial obligation to maintain the child; and

(b)

apportion that obligation between
the spouses according to their relative abilities to contribute to the
performance of the obligation."

The principal point of disagreement between the
parties is the fact that the wife works in a day care center earning $300 per
month rather than as a registered nurse earning $3,000 per month.

The husband submits that the wife could resume her
nursing career with little or no re‑training simply by re‑applying
for registered status and then seeking employment. If she did so, the higher
income from nursing would help promote her economic self‑sufficiency and
would allow her to make a greater contribution to the joint obligation to
support the children of the marriage. He maintains that a review of his
financial statements reveals that he cannot support the children at an
acceptable level and remain solvent without a commitment by the wife to fulfill
her duty to help maintain the children to the best of her ability.

For her part, the wife submits that she sacrificed her
career advancement to that of her husband so that she ought to be supported by
maintenance until she can become self‑sufficient. She says that it is
impossible for her to re‑qualify as a registered nurse and, because of
her back problem, to do the work of a nurse. She feels that she is doing the
best she can by working in day care centers, by trying to improve the kind of
positions which are available, and by studying to improve her child care
qualifications.

The wife made a decision with respect to her back problem,
which has been diagnosed as a lumbar disc protrusion. An orthopaedic surgeon
recommended a myelogram which, if it resulted in the detection of a specific
lesion, would probably be followed by surgical discoidectomy. She decided not
to proceed with surgery because of the risks involved nothwithstanding that the
surgeon expressed his opinion that it would be in her best interest to have
that investigation.

I find it difficult to fault the decision she has
made. While another person might have made a different decision, it is
desirable that a person have the right to control his or her own body. The
person whose body it is will have to live with the consequences of the
decision, perhaps for the rest of his or her life. Others must abide by the
decision made.

Although I do not accept that the wife sacrificed her
career advancement for her husband, of which there is no evidence whatsoever,
it is clear that she is, and will be, unable to resume a career in nursing in
her present physical condition. The Court therefore accepts that she is doing
the best she can in the present circumstances.

That is an important fact in determining the level and
duration of maintenance. However, there exists another fact which is even more
important.

The husband says that he is unable to continue paying
maintenance at its current level. It is necessary for him to re‑pay his
business debts in priority to all other expenses or else there is a probability
that he will lose his partnership and, therefore, he will have to try to obtain
employment which will provide him with a substantially reduced income. In such
case, he will be unable to pay maintenance or, if so, it will be much less than
the present amount. I find that the evidence supports this submission.

The short‑term consequence of continuing
maintenance at its present level will adversely affect the husband's long‑term
ability to pay or pay at the present level. I find that it is in the best
interest of the children and the wife that the requirements of the long term
take priority over the advantages of the short term.

I find that maintenance will be reduced to $1,400 per
month. The husband shall pay at that rate for a period of 2 years so that he
will have funds with which to reduce his business debts. At the end of that
period, the husband shall resume paying maintenance at the current level or at
such level as may be ordered at that time by a court of competent jurisdiction.

RELIGIOUS UPBRINGING

The parties have agreed between themselves that the
wife will have custody of the 2 children and that the husband will have liberal
access to them. The agreement as to custody ordinarily assures that the
children will be brought up in the religion of the wife as the custodial
parent: see
Henderson v. Henderson

(1977),
29 R.F.L. 1 (B.C. Prov. Ct.)
;

Gunn v. Gunn

(1975),
1975 CanLII 1938 (PE PC)
,
24 R.F.L. 182 (P.E.I. S.C.)
;
Brown v. Brown

(1983),
1983 CanLII 2311 (SK CA)
,
39 R.F.L. (2d) 396 (Sask. C.A.)
; and
Fougere v. Fougere
(1987),

1987 CanLII 7842 (NB CA)
,
6 R.F.L. (3d) 314 (N.B. C.A.)
.

The wife has also agreed that the children will have
an opportunity to be exposed to the religion of the husband. If it had not been
agreed upon, the Court could have ordered it:
see
Pfeifer v. Pfeifer

(1982),
1982 CanLII 2358 (SK QB)
,
28 R.F.L. (2d) 236 (Sask. Q.B.)
at p.245
.

The husband is Jewish, but does not actively attend
synagogue. However, it is submitted on his behalf that he is a conscious member
of the Jewish community.

The wife was born Catholic, but converted to Judaism
shortly before her marriage. She testified that she never practised Judaism.
She attended, church and now considers herself to be a Catholic once again.

The husband believes that the children were born
Jewish. They were circumcised according to Jewish rites. He assumed that they
would be brought up Jewish. But there has been no formal Jewish religious
education. The family has held a Passover seder and celebrated Hanukkah. They
also celebrated Christmas. The husband testified that, when things got nasty
between himself and his wife, she told him that she had secretly arranged for
the children to be baptised. The husband also testified that the older son had
told him that he had been taken to church and Sunday school.

She intends to raise the boys as Roman Catholics.
However, she is not adverse to their learning about their Jewish heritage. She
has agreed to expose them to Judaism. But he wants more. He wants each of them
to become a bar mitzvah. Since she will not agree to this, he requests the
Court to order it as a condition of custody and access.

A Jewish boy reaches his religious majority upon
reaching his 13th birthday. At that time he assumes responsibility for the
observance of all precepts and commandments. Bar mitzvah means 'subject to the
commandments'. To mark the occasion, it is customary for the boy to celebrate
by simply reciting appropriate benedictions in the synagogue. Sometimes a boy
may study for a year or more and conduct the whole of the synagogue service.

He gives 2 reasons for his request. He wants the
children to know and appreciate Jewish tradition and culture. He also wants
them to understand anti‑Semitism which they, as Jews, will inevitably
meet sooner or later. However, the wife feels that it is unfair to the children
to require them to participate in preparation and a ceremony which would
distinguish them from their friends.

It is submitted on behalf of the wife that the
question to be answered is whether either party is considered in law to occupy
a superior position with regard to determining the religious upbringing of the
children of the marriage. That question has a relatively simple and
straightforward answer. At common law, the father generally had the absolute
right to determine the religious faith and education of his children. That
right now rests with both parents; see Bromley,
Family Law
(Butterworth,
1971, 4th. Ed.) p.301 and Davies,
Family Law in Canada
(Carswell, 1984)
p.527.

However, with respect, that is not the correct question.
The issue to be determined is whether this Court can and should order in the
corollary relief judgment to be issued that each of the the 2 male children of
the marriage become a bar mitzvah at age 13. Whether the Court has the power
and jurisdiction to grant such an order is easy to answer. Whether such an
order should be granted in this particular case is more difficult.

There is no doubt that this Court has the jurisdiction
to make the order sought. It is an aspect of the Court's inherent
parens

patriae
jurisdiction. It is also an aspect of the Court's statutory
jurisdiction set out in
s.16
of the
Divorce Act
, 1985.
That provision
authorizes a court of competent jurisdiction to make an order respecting
custody or access and, in exercise of that power, it will take into
consideration only the best interests of the child as determined by reference
to the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of the child.

It is the duty of the Court to decide what is in the
best interests of the children. In order to do that, the Court must examine
their condition, means, needs and other circumstances.

The children are, and will be, living with their
mother. They are both of tender age. What little religious upbringing they have
had to date has been Catholic. Their ages suggest that they have not had the
opportunity to develop deep religious convictions and beliefs. That, no doubt,
will change as time goes by. At some point of time, they will doubtless be
mature enough to make a meaningful contribution to any decision as to their
religious upbringing.

The Court may give a child of appropriate age an
opportunity to be heard as to his or her religious faith: see
C.G.H. v.
A.B.H.

(1976),
1976 CanLII 2535 (NS SC)
,
22 N.S.R. (2d) 67 (N.S.S.C.)
. For that reason, I considered
the desirability of delaying the making of the decision until the boys are
closer to age 13 (perhaps at age 11). But, in the intervening years, they would
be residing with their mother who would naturally direct their religious
upbringing in a particular direction so that delaying the decision for several
years would have the same effect as making a decision now in favour of the
position advanced on behalf of the wife. I have come to the conclusion that an
immediate decision is desirable because it will conclude this adjudication in a
more honest and straightforward way and without unnecessary delay.

The Court is not called upon to decide the question of
custody. The parties were able to agree upon that matter. It is submitted on
behalf of the wife that the parties' agreement as to custody has in effect
settled the matter of bar mitzvahs because the custodial parent generally has
the right to direct the religious upbringing of the children unless that would
be damaging to them. On the other hand, it is submitted on behalf of the
husband that the agreement by the wife to expose them to the religion of the
non‑custodial father has in effect settled the matter of bar mitzvahs
because such agreement can best be fulfilled by the wife giving the children
the opportunity to gain some real knowledge and sense of the father's religion
by studying it and participating in it. I cannot see that this course of action
would be damaging to the children. It may be incongruous to study Roman
Catholicism and Judaism at the same time, and it may be inconvenient for
children to study these religions during their formative years, but it should
give them an understanding and tolerance that is all too rare in this day and
age.

The Court hesitates to rely upon the sincerity of the
wife. Her conversion to Judaism immediately before marriage apparently led the
husband to believe that any children born of the marriage would be brought up
in that faith. Her return to Catholicism sometime after marriage, the secrecy
of arrangements for baptism, and the lack of consultation before taking the
children to church and Sunday school all go to create a real doubt about the
depth of her commitment to expose the children to the faith of the husband.

After lengthy consideration, I have decided that it is
in the best interests of the 2 children of the marriage that they become bar
mitzvah as each reaches 13 years of age. This decision has nothing whatsoever
to do with the Court choosing between different faiths or religions, which the
Court will not do: see
In re J. M. Carroll
,
[1931] 1 K.B. 317 (C.A.)
;
and
Re Custody of Pamela A.

(1969),
1969 CanLII 1587 (NS SC)
,
1 N.S.R. (2d) 232 (N.S.S.C.)
. It has
to do, rather, with giving the children the opportunity to know 2 different
(and, at the same time, not so different) faiths so that they can learn from
both and, perhaps, in the fullness of time, they may be able to choose what
religious convictions and beliefs they want to guide their lives.

The corollary relief judgment to be issued will
include a direction to the parents to encourage and to give the 2 children the
opportunity to study and celebrate their bar mitzvahs. It is hoped that the
parents will be able to agree on all necessary details. But, if not, either
party will be at liberty to apply to the Family Court for appropriate
directions from time to time.

SUMMARY and CONCLUSION

Matrimonial assets will be divided 70% to the wife and
30% to the husband, in accordance with the directions hereinbefore set forth.

The husband will pay periodic maintenance for the
support of the wife and children in the amount of $1,400 per month, payable in
the same manner as at present or, if that is in doubt, ½ on the 15th. day and ½
on the last day of each month hereafter, commencing in the month of January,
1991.

Both parties will give each of the children the
opportunity to study and celebrate a bar mitzvah and will encourage them in
that regard.

The
separation agreement entered into by the parties will be incorporated into the
corollary relief judgment.

Each
party will bear his or her own costs.

J.

Halifax,
Nova Scotia December 28, 1990
